result.summary: Hercules is denied Iole, then kills Iphitus in a fit of madness and is struck with disease. After a clash with Apollo at Delphi he is sold to Omphale, and later sacks Troy, giving Hesione to Telamon.

scenes.title: The archery contest for Iole
scenes.summary: Hercules wins the contest at Oechalia but is refused Iole, though Iphitus supports him.
scenes.stakes: Hercules stands to lose a bride and his honour.

scenes.title: Murder of Iphitus
scenes.summary: Iphitus seeks Hercules' help over stolen cattle, and Hercules in madness throws him from the walls of Tiryns.
scenes.stakes: Iphitus risks his life; Hercules risks guilt for murder.

scenes.title: Purification and Delphi
scenes.summary: Refused by Neleus, Hercules is purified by Deiphobus, then tries to seize the Delphic tripod and fights Apollo until Zeus intervenes. The oracle orders him sold into slavery.
scenes.stakes: Hercules suffers disease and risks divine punishment.

scenes.title: Servitude to Omphale
scenes.summary: Sold by Hermes to Omphale, Hercules performs deeds, including killing Syleus, burying Icarus and being tricked by Daedalus' statue.
scenes.stakes: Hercules must serve as a slave to cure his disease.

scenes.title: Sack of Troy
scenes.summary: Hercules sails against Laomedon, takes Ilium, rewards Telamon with Hesione, and Podarces is ransomed as Priam.
scenes.stakes: Laomedon's city and family face destruction; Telamon risks Hercules' jealous wrath.

alias_notes.explanation: Podarces got the name Priam, from the Greek for 'to ransom', after Hesione ransomed him.

notable_quotes.reason: Telamon cleverly averts Hercules' jealous rage by flattering him.

analysis.text: Hercules' violence leads to guilt, disease and slavery, showing that even heroes must atone for killing, especially breaking guest-friendship.
The passage links Hercules to many places and heroes, stitching local legends into one Greek mythic timeline.

legacy.text: The story of Hercules serving Omphale, often shown in cross-dressing, became a favourite subject in Renaissance and Baroque art.

fun_facts.text: The Library is attributed to Apollodorus but was probably written in the first or second century AD.

language_notes.text: "Vanquish himself and his sons" means defeat Eurytus and his sons; the contest was set so that Hercules had to beat the host's whole family.
"Kine" is an archaic plural for cattle.
"Was fain to" means was eager or willing to, here with the sense of being driven to do something.
The tripod was the seat of the Pythian priestess at Delphi; seizing it meant claiming the power to give oracles.
The Cercopes were mischievous thieves who plagued travellers; the myth is told in more detail elsewhere.
Telamon's trick works because an altar to Hercules as victor flatters him; the stones are what he pretends to be gathering.
The name Priam is explained by a Greek verb meaning "to buy" (priamai), making the ransom the origin of the name.

context_notes.text: Hercules had earlier killed his own children in a fit of madness, which is why Eurytus fears for any future offspring.
Pylos was the kingdom of Neleus, father of Nestor.
Omphale, queen of Lydia, is the mistress in the best-known story of Hercules' servitude.
Ilium is another name for Troy. Hercules attacks Laomedon, who had earlier cheated him of a promised reward.

literary_notes.text: Iphitus trusted Hercules as a friend and is killed by him as a guest, a grim reversal of hospitality.
The great hero, famed for strength, is fooled by a statue and attacks a lifeless image.
Hercules' jealous readiness to attack an ally shows his violent pride and touchy honour.
